302.title: A very narrow bridge
302.hook: Rebbe Nachman: the whole world is a very narrow bridge, and the main thing is not to be afraid
302.howItsDone: The song Kol ha-olam kulo, set to Rebbe Nachman's words, is sung at weddings, camps, memorials and gatherings; Breslov Hasidim study his teachings in Likutei Moharan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tailor made his accounting with God on Yom Kippur. Your line was let's call it even. Did you tell one honest truth, kindly? Day three hundred two.

Go to almost any Jewish wedding, summer camp or youth group, and at some point people put their arms around each other's shoulders and sway, singing a slow Hebrew song. Kol ha-olam kulo, gesher tzar me'od. The whole world is a very narrow bridge. And the main thing is not to be afraid at all. Millions of people know the tune. Far fewer know where the words come from: a Hasidic master who died young, who wrote openly about sadness, and whose actual words are a little different from the song. Today: the bridge.
screen: `ARMS AROUND SHOULDERS, SWAYING.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD IS A NARROW BRIDGE.` → `WHERE DO THE WORDS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Rebbe Nachman of Breslov was born in 1772, a great-grandson of the Baal Shem Tov, whose stories we've been hearing. He lived in Ukraine and died at thirty-eight, in the town of Uman. His student Nathan wrote down his teachings in a great book called Likutei Moharan. In one passage, Rebbe Nachman says, roughly: know that a person has to cross a very, very narrow bridge, and the rule and the main thing is not to frighten yourself at all. Nearly two hundred years later, a songwriter turned that into the song, and changed it a little on the way. The song says the whole world is the bridge. And the song says, don't be afraid. The original is subtler. The Hebrew verb is reflexive: don't make yourself afraid. Fear will come. It comes to everyone standing over a drop. What you can refuse to do is feed it, to stand there frightening yourself with every way you might fall. Notice what the teaching doesn't say. It doesn't say the bridge is wide. It doesn't say you won't wobble. It says the path really is narrow, and you still have to cross it. Rebbe Nachman knew this from inside. He spoke often of his own heaviness of spirit, and he also taught that it is a great mitzvah to be joyful always. Not because life is easy, but because joy is how you keep walking. So the bridge isn't a promise of safety. It's permission to be scared and move anyway.
screen: `NACHMAN OF BRESLOV, 1772–1810.` · `A VERY, VERY NARROW BRIDGE.` · `DON'T MAKE YOURSELF AFRAID.` · `SCARED, AND WALKING ANYWAY.` · then, large: `NOT AFRAID AT ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one step in spite of fear. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been avoiding because it scares you. A phone call. A doctor's appointment. An apology. A conversation. Don't try to stop being afraid of it. Just notice the fear, and notice when you start frightening yourself with stories about how it'll go. Now picture only the first step. Not the whole bridge. One plank. See yourself taking it. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to take it. The bell holds the time.
A very narrow bridge. Rebbe Nachman's picture of life: the way across is narrow, and the main thing is not to make yourself afraid.
Your line: not afraid at all. Today, when fear shows up, don't argue with it. Just stop feeding it, and take the first step. Day three hundred two.

myth: the song's words are exactly what Rebbe Nachman wrote
the original says a person must cross a narrow bridge and not frighten himself. the song reshaped it.
Rebbe Nachman taught that it's a great mitzvah to be joyful always
and he spoke honestly about his own sadness too.
the teaching promises the bridge is safe
it says the way is narrow, and asks you to cross anyway.

fork.setup: you're halfway across a very narrow bridge and fear rises. what does Rebbe Nachman's teaching ask?
options: turn back until the fear is gone.
don't feed the fear. keep walking.
fork.reveal: his verb is reflexive: don't make yourself afraid. fear may come, but you don't have to frighten yourself further.

original.note: Hebrew: a very narrow bridge, from Rebbe Nachman's teaching in Likutei Moharan.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice song about not being scared.
what it means: life is narrow and wobbly, and you cross it anyway without feeding your fear.
what a scholar hears: Likutei Moharan II:48 uses a reflexive verb, yitpached, don't frighten yourself, and speaks of a person crossing, not the whole world being the bridge.

sources.work: Likutei Moharan (Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, recorded by Nathan of Nemirov)
